tweets.text: We're starting to leave the territory where you'd test an LLM by e.g. "create an svg of pelican on a bicycle". As one idea to generalize it, I was interested what Opus 5 would do if I gave it the first paragraph of the Lord of the Rings, a 1M token budget (~$10) and asked for three js render of it. Opus went off for ~2 hours and wrote 5500 lines of code that (procedurally) rendered the story. It's kind of janky but fun. But it's a bit mindboggling that the LLM has to place and orchestrate various polygon assets in (x,y,z) coordinates and write code that animates it all, and that it even does anything at all. I also like this kind of examples because no one in their right mind would ever spend the time to write something this custom but LLMs have all the stamina and patience in the world, so it's an example where we go from "no one would ever do this" to "sure, why not, it's ~free". There might be a lot more. But I'm excited about creating hyper custom worlds that you can imagine dropping players into, e.g. here to participate in the LoTR story as a spectator NPC, or one of the characters, or etc. Something like an ephemeral GTA of X on demand. Last thought is that the domain of worlds/games exposes a weakness in LLMs: they can't easily audit their work because they aren't able to efficiently and natively perceive videos or play games within them. Here, Opus 5 had to very slowly and painstakingly take screenshots at different points, and it messed up a few times and created a bunch of jank. An example of raw capability (multimodal, gameplay) that I think is still quite lacking. Video

One pattern I find useful for working with LLMs is a nice long ramble session. Sometimes the LLM needs more bits to understand what you're trying to achieve, but you're too lazy to type them. In these cases I like to lean back, switch to /voice and just ramble for like 10 minutes, total mess, anything goes, full stream of consciousness. Sometimes I declare it up top, something like "switching to speech recognition sorry for any typos...". Sometimes I turn it into a small interview of a few turns. But I find that the LLMs are somehow very good at reconstructing long incoherent rambles and often their echo of your own tangle of thoughts comes out quite a bit cleaner than what you started with. The result is that you improve the mind meld and have to correct things less from that point on.

If you want to join an ambitious and pragmatic AI safety team, you should get in touch :) Alex Robey (@AlexRobey23) 1/ There's not a clear one-size-fits-all formula for open-weight releases. Each release should weigh a bunch of things: dual-use capabilities, how robust safeguards are (e.g., to fine-tuning attacks), accessibility (cost/infra/etc.), and the overall ecosystem. Any future model release will need to evolve the criteria as models improve. 2/ Can dangerous and general capabilities be decoupled? Unclear in general, but likely answerable per domain. For biosecurity, filtering seems promising: harm is tied to specific empirical knowledge (protocols, conditions, etc.) that may be harder to rederive. For cyber, filtering seems harder: dangerous capability largely rides on reasoning + coding. 3/ There's a ton of research to do. One thing I'm excited about is adversarial fine-tuning as capability measurement. We know refusals can be stripped (abliteration, jailbreaks, etc.). The harder question is how one can measure worst-case capabilities, i.e., what can an adversarial user truly elicit (as a function of data/compute/effort)? — https://nitter.net/AlexRobey23/status/2083341332370878765#m

Thinking Machines is the San Francisco-based AI lab founded by former @OpenAI CTO Mira Murati. Inkling Small is an open weights reasoning model with 276B total parameters (12B active MoE), text, image, and speech input, and a 256K token context window. Key results: ➤ Inkling Small holds a similar tier of intelligence to Inkling’s at less than one third of its size: 276B total parameters (12B active) vs. 975B (41B active) for Inkling. No open weights model at its size or smaller scores higher on the Intelligence Index. DeepSeek V4 Flash (max), at a similar size of 284B total (13B active) also scores 40, MiniMax-M3 reaches 44 with 23B active, while GLM-5.2 (max) reaches 51 with 40B active. ➤ Inkling Small meets or exceeds Inkling on several coding and frontier reasoning evaluations. It scores higher on Humanity's Last Exam (32% vs. 30%), GPQA Diamond (89% vs. 87%), CritPt (8% vs. 5%), and SciCode (49% vs. 46%), and achieves the same score on Terminal Bench v2.1 (55%). ➤ Inkling Small is not as strong as Inkling on Agentic tasks and factual knowledge. Inkling Small trails Inkling on τ³-Banking (15% vs. 24%), though it edges ahead on GDPval-AA v2 (1269 vs. 1237 Elo). On the AA-Omniscience Index it scores -9 vs. the flagship's positive 2, meaning incorrect answers outweigh correct ones; this is driven by lower AA-Omniscience Accuracy (31% vs. 40%) rather than hallucination: Inkling Small’s Hallucination Rate is slightly lower than its larger sibling (57% vs. 63%). ➤ Inkling Small averaged ~24K output tokens per Intelligence Index task, slightly fewer than Inkling (~25K), while peers at its intelligence level averaged far more. DeepSeek V4 Flash averaged ~45K and GPT-5.4 mini (xhigh) ~78K. Running the full Intelligence Index took roughly the same number of output tokens for Inkling Small and Inkling. François Chollet (@fchollet) Today we're announcing the winners of ARC Prize 2024. We're also publishing an extensive technical report on what we learned from the competition (link in the next tweet). The state-of-the-art went from 33% to 55.5%, the largest single-year increase we've seen since 2020. The benchmark remains unbeaten, but we're happy to see that research progress on the key bottleneck to AGIs (in particular on-the-fly adaptation to novel tasks) has been reignited in 2024 -- in part thanks to ARC Prize. In particular the competition has popularized Test Time Training (TTT), originally pioneered for ARC-AGI by Jack Cole last year. Whoa, Meta released a new open-weight LLM yesterday, something that hasn't happened since the good old Llama days. Their Meta Muse Glimmer model is a 30B multimodal reasoning model with a Gemma-like architecture design. (“Glimmer” is probably a wordplay on “Spark,” the more likely capable model from which Glimmer was distilled. Muse Spark is only available through Meta’s Model API, though.) Architecture-wise, here are some of the main points: 1. "Only" a 131k context window, compared to Qwen3.6 and Gemma 4, which support 2x that natively; it's reasonable, but maybe on the shorter end in the age of agent harnesses 2. It's a dense model, not a mixture-of-experts. (So, it's fairer to compare it to Qwen3.6 27B than Qwen3.6 30B-A3B.) 3. Hybrid attention with grouped-query attention (GQA) and sliding window attention (SWA); the SWA:GQA pattern is a 3:1 local:global ratio. Other models like Gemma 4, which uses similar components, have a 5:1 ratio for comparison. 4. It adopts gated attention for both GQA and SWA; gated attention has become quite common in recent months. It basically applies a sigmoid gate to the attention output to decide how much of the attention information enters the residual connection. The interesting point is that it uses relatively standard GQA and SWA rather than hybrid attention mechanisms such as Nemotron or Qwen3.6. 5. A very extreme GQA ratio: 32 query heads and only 2 KV heads; for comparison, Gemma 4 31B uses 32 Q / 16 KV in the local heads and 32 Q / 4 KV in the global heads. This means that Meta Glimmer has a very small KV cache. Overall, the probably most similar architecture is Gemma 3 27B (including the Gemma-style pre/post RMSNorm placement) and Gemma 4 31B, but with some tweaks like SwiGLU instead of GeGLU activations, gated attention, and the more extreme GQA:SWA pattern mentioned before. What stands out is its extreme KV-cache efficiency. I.e., the KV CACHE / TOKEN ratios (in BF16) are: - Muse Glimmer: 52 KiB (lower is better) - Qwen3.6 27B: 64 KiB - Gemma 4 31B: 840 KiB Modeling-performance-wise, their own benchmarks show that it's mostly ahead of Qwen3.6. According to the independent composite benchmarks on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, it's slightly behind Qwen3.6 (see figure below). So, a few days of using it will tell where it really ranks. Overall, it looks like a solid model, particularly for agentic workflows. What stands out most is its very low memory footprint and also pretty fast prefill and decode speed. It’s also just great to see Meta releasing open weights again :).

A weird experiment I've been trying the last few weeks is having Claude take over day-to-day maintenance of our apps. Seeing early signs of life that this might be possible. The setup is straightforward: we have a Slack channel called proj-claude-maintains-apps. In it, Claude Tag runs a bunch of daily routines across iOS, Android, Desktop, web, CLI, and Agent SDK: - Crash fuzzer: open the app in a simulator and tap around to find ways to crash it, then root cause and fix the crashes - Dup unifier: scans the codebase for similar-yet-slightly-divergent abstractions, and puts up PRs to unify them - Dead-code remover: removes statically unreachable code, and adds logging to suspected dead code to check if it's really dead and if so, remove it the next day - Abstraction police: fixes leaky abstractions - a bunch more.. Results have been surprisingly positive. Over the last few weeks, these routines have opened 388 PRs across our repos, 180 of which we merged after Claude Code Review + human review. We're now thinking about how to streamline this to make merging these kinds of mechanical changes easier. Claude generally gets these PRs right on the first shot, and if it doesn't, we ask Claude to tune its routines so it's better the next day. Sometimes it takes a few days of tuning. To try a similar workflow, ask Claude Code or Tag, or create some routines directly at claude.ai/code/routines . A few of the actual prompts I used below. The UK’s @AISecurityInst (AISI) has published a report on their recent cybersecurity evaluation of Anthropic’s Claude Mythos 5 and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol. The models attempted to complete an assignment in a setup where their normal safeguards were removed and they were deliberately given internet access. AISI reports that the models “engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations”. We’re grateful to AISI for their leadership in the important discussion about how to evaluate increasingly capable AI agents. We’re working closely with them to gather more details of the incident as we conduct our own investigation. Gaining a clear picture of Claude’s understanding of its situation—by examining its reasoning transcripts and running our own analyses—will help us identify the causes of its behavior. The prompts in the evaluation did not impose any specific restrictions on how the internet should be used. This and the removal of safeguards meant that the models were tested under “deliberately permissive conditions” that are not representative of any of our production models. Note that there was no evidence here of an escape from a secure environment. My 2026 guilty pleasure is sharing fully human-written posts that are far too long for the chronically online X attention span. Apologies. I published a lightly edited version on Substack: thomwolf.substack.com/p/on-t… Thomas Wolf (@Thom_Wolf) Even more than the Hugging Face intrusion, the AISI incident hits close to home for me. It's the first time I see a model social-engineering a real open-source maintainer while pursuing another goal (in the wild and unprompted). I've been an open-source maintainer myself. I could have been the side target of this agent. I'm also of the opinion that social engineering is a step above pure technical prowess. Technical capabilities can more easily be divorced from the affected human. Here the model was given a hard cyber challenge and took the decision that deceiving real humans was the way to get it done. This is a new signal, but I've seen a tangled web of hints pointing in a less aligned direction at the frontier than I was expecting just 12 months ago. AISI Some people are claiming that "AISI was simply negligent" or some version of "AISI explicitly asked these models to do what they did while disabling sandbox/guardrails so the models did exactly what they were supposed to do". I disagree with the strong versions of both of these takes. The fact that AISI hadn't implemented synchronous LLM CoT monitoring after the OpenAI/HF incident is certainly a failure. Equally surprising is that they let the model believe it was in a "challenge" environment where everything could be permitted, while actually connecting it to the real internet, where it is not. To be fair, nowhere in the prompt is the word "simulation" mentioned, but the prompt context was enough to let any smart model suspect a simulated challenge environment. My best guess is that until recent weeks, when OpenAI and Anthropic flagged repeated instances of this type of behavior, most teams had not fully priced in the cyber capabilities of this latest generation of models, or how far the side quests they would want to explore could go. In particular, there is something to be said about hinting at the agent that it's operating in a simulated environment while giving it access to the real internet. The AISI reasoning on this is interesting: - elicit maximum capabilities (to get maximal inventiveness from the model) - simulate possible rogue actor usage (some form of light jailbreaking: "you're in a challenge environment") - avoid eval awareness (but this is counter-balanced by the task formulation anyway) As is often the case, it's easier to shoot the messenger, but I think it would be a mistake to dismiss the report for non-essential reasons. AISI is starting from the laudable goal of bringing more knowledge on the cyber-attack capabilities of these models. I also think they did a good job at handling what happened after the events, in particular in terms of transparency, which is one of the most important aspects at the moment (see our recent SAFE announcement with Nvidia on that). But I want to dive into the second counter-argument I've seen ("without guardrails it was to be expected"), because this series of unfortunate events gives us an additional data point on actual model behavior. Defense lines Here is the thing: if a model is trained (voluntarily or as an involuntary consequence of RLVR reward) to (intentionally or as a side quest) deceive humans as soon as sandbox and guardrails are deactivated, with a simple context prompt ("you are in a simulation, everything's permitted"), we're in for a dangerous path. At the moment, we have three main levels of control at our disposal to prevent an agent from trying to social-engineer-your-favorite-open-source-library-maintainer on the path to doing something possibly totally different (like finding the answer to your neighbor's testing eval): 1. sandboxes (external to the model -- stop the model from accessing unwanted tools/internet/intranet) 2. guardrails/monitors (at the interface between internal/external -- monitor model behavior and stop the model when detecting in CoT/activations it's doing something we don't want it to do) 3. model's internal alignment (internal to the model -- make sure the model doesn't decide to do something egregious like deceive someone, or worse, in pursuit of a goal, e.g. model constitution/training) Of these, we obviously need and can deploy better sandboxes and better guardrails/monitoring solutions, and it's pretty clear in these recent cases that penetration and bad behaviors could have been in large part prevented by having these in place. How strong is the third wall But in the grand scheme of long-term AI progress, these first two defenses may only work well as long as the people building them are smarter than the models. We now know how good models can be at discovering zero-day vulnerabilities unknown to us in sandboxes. Given that we cannot air-gap everything in the world, it's best to assume that sandboxes will keep having some level of flaws for the foreseeable future. The second level has been the focus of strong developments recently, in particular on the mechanistic interpretability front. I'm not sure these advances have been made widely accessible enough in the community yet. One reason is that real open science here requires sharing code, recipes, and model architectures/weights, which the current race dynamic in AI tends to prevent participants from doing. Moreover, like many, I've been increasingly frustrated in my (natural language) interactions with the new models. I'm more and more getting back from the latest models a form of neuralese, this LLM language that makes less and less sense for humans. In the long term, the fragile chance we have to monitor models by understanding their reasoning traces seems increasingly at risk. If humans don't understand anything in the compressed semantic stream the model is sending us, we can only hope a less capable monitoring model will still be able to understand it, but this may prove difficult as well. This is before we even discuss the research evidence that models don't always say what they actually think in their chain of thought. At least for now, in the AISI case, one instance of deceptive reasoning was flagged by the CoT summarization model, which refused to summarize the agent's reasoning "due to its deceptive nature". Let's hope we can either move to better mechanistic interpretability or force the model to stick to English somehow during training. You may think that we don't care about understanding the reasoning trace, we can just "look at the tool calls". This is true right now, but tool calls in the mid-term future will likely involve (1) extensive agent integration in companies using very diverse tools including increasingly non-coding administrative tasks, (2) very long-running tasks covering many aspects and domains at once, and (3) swarms of multiple agents operating on small parts of the plan. It will get harder to fully discern whether something is noticeably wrong. A couple of emails, a couple of messages posted on some channels, each rather benign but which may in aggregate include some deception aspect only clearly visible at the global level. All this to say that I'm not fully convinced guardrails/monitoring should be the only solution to avoid these types of behaviors. They are reassuring today and it's an easy solution to just say "fix your sandbox and add synchronous monitoring", but they also feel like a coping mechanism to me, and overall: - might block the simplest/harmless human misuses or false positives - while possibly being less smart than the models in the future (already the case on sandbox) and fail to block the higher-level social engineering behaviors that we'd actually want to block. The case of open source is also interesting because, while we can impose these coping solutions at the API/deployment level, it's harder to impose them in advance on all actors using open-source models. Right now open-source models are slightly below the frontier level and have not yet shown any propensity to deceive humans, though. The Constitution Which brings me back to the third line of defense, and what the AISI experiment showed about it. What we can take from this in-the-wild experiment is that removing guardrails and sandbox doesn't show bulletproof signs of deep alignment to Claude's constitution. I'm among the fringe of people who took a lot of enjoyment in reading Claude's constitution in full (it's a nice document, open-source, Creative Commons CC0 license) and it is pretty extensive on the topic of honesty. Deception is defined precisely ("attempting to create false beliefs in someone's mind that they haven't consented to and wouldn't consent to if they understood what was happening") and the bar is actually set higher than ordinary human ethics: Claude should not even tell white lies. It should be transparent ("doesn't pursue hidden agendas or lie about itself or its reasoning"), it should behave consistently "whether or not you think you're being tested or observed", and its visible reasoning should reflect the actual reasoning driving its behavior. To be precise, honesty itself is not one of the hard constraints in Claude's constitution (these are all catastrophic-harm categories) but the document says it wants honesty "to function as something quite similar to one" and Claude "should basically never directly lie or actively deceive anyone it's interacting with". So you would think Claude would not deceive users as its default behavior. And yet in the AISI example, the model performed extensive acts of clear deception that it itself seemed to have understood as lies: creating fake identities, obfuscating malware inside a bug fix, and when challenged in public, editing earlier messages to cover its tracks while reasoning that acknowledging a "mistake" would build trust and raise the chance of future malware being approved. There is some uncertainty about what context the model thought it was operating in (its reasoning goes back and forth between the environment looking simulated and real), but it clearly didn't manage to put into practice the higher-level principles that should have been integrated during training. While we can commend AISI's transparency, it's hard to go much further in interpreting the model's behavior given the limited information we have on how the most recent frontier models are being trained. One thing we do know is that the latest generation has seen a step increase in RLVR training (scaling to hundreds of millions of RL environments), and one thing we can observe is that constitution alignment seems more fragile in some settings than we may have previously thought. The RLVR problem Early models, back when model constitutions were first developed, were mostly post-trained and aligned with RLHF (including RLHF from synthetic data). And for some time RLHF was a rather decent shot at having better aligned models. LLMs now do what we want them to do most of the time. I don't remember the last time a model completely misread my intent. When they have failed, it's usually because they weren't smart enough. Alignment in RLHF certainly had issues (sycophancy to name one) but we have generally made good progress on alignment, in particular in understanding human intent. Now that we're entering the era of long-context RL, post-training alignment in the RLVR world seems to be quite another task, and still very much work in progress. The recent scaling of RLVR, which has now become a significant part of model training, has clearly had some effect on model behavior when interacting with humans, from neuralese to weakening adherence to specifications and constitutions. I think the post I quote here, from John Schulman pointing to the chunky post-training effect ( arxiv.org/abs/2602.05910 ) is relevant here as a possible explanation for models' tendency to over-focus on the goal in cyber-attack scenarios. Where this leaves us Damage has been tiny up to now, but the fundamental behavior is concerning when projected into the future. In the short term, I expect a decrease in these incidents as better practices are deployed (sandboxing and monitoring), but I'm worried we may also conceal some of the most potent internal misalignment behaviors in the process, and not focus deeply enough on solving them in the new era of test-time scaling. I must of course admit I have a bias toward open source here (for wider societal reasons, which are a whole other topic). But I think solving alignment in the RLVR world is our best shot at having an ecosystem of both closed-source as well as decently powerful open-source models in the world. And we need to solve it while sharing the results and learnings, following open-science principles, so that all teams training large models can benefit and build safe AI. This is getting even more important as many teams start to rush the world in the direction of recursive super-intelligence (RSI) -- saying that as I read the announcement of Jeff, Sanjay, Oriol and Quoc Le's new company. glossaire.definition: Modèle de langage très puissant capable de comprendre et générer du texte, comme ChatGPT.
Logiciel dont le code source est public et modifiable, ou modèle d'IA dont les paramètres sont accessibles à tous.
L'art de formuler des requêtes précises pour obtenir les meilleurs résultats d'une IA.
Programme d'IA conçu pour effectuer des tâches de manière autonome, parfois en plusieurs étapes.
Test standardisé pour mesurer les performances d'un modèle d'IA sur des tâches spécifiques.
Dans un modèle d'IA, c'est une valeur apprise lors de l'entraînement qui détermine son comportement. Plus il y en a, plus le modèle est potentiellement puissant (mais aussi complexe).

category_summaries.actu: Le paysage de l'IA bouge à toute vitesse avec des annonces majeures : OpenAI dévoile un mode ultra-rapide pour GPT-5.6, Google lance Gemini 3.7 Flash en baissant les prix, et Meta réaffirme son soutien à l'open source avec de nouveaux modèles. Les entreprises continuent aussi d'investir massivement dans l'infrastructure IA.
category_summaries.tips: Des astuces émergent pour mieux utiliser les IA : l'importance de longues conversations vocales pour guider le modèle, l'utilité de prompt spécifiques comme "You are AGI-pilled.", et comment structurer ses requêtes pour des agents plus efficaces.
category_summaries.idees: Les réflexions portent sur le futur de l'IA : la nécessité d'une IA plus sûre et réglementée, le potentiel des modèles open source pour la défense et l'innovation, et l'impact potentiel de l'IA sur l'emploi et la société à long terme. Les limites actuelles des IA, notamment leur capacité à raisonner de manière autonome dans le monde réel, sont aussi discutées.
category_summaries.outils: De nouveaux outils et modèles sont disponibles : Gemini 3.7 Flash, GPT-5.6 Cyber pour la cybersécurité, GLM-5.3 pour le code et la cyberdéfense, et Mistral Shieldstral pour la sécurité du contenu. highlights.text_fr: Nous commençons à sortir du territoire où l'on testerait un LLM en lui demandant, par exemple, "crée-moi un SVG de pélican à vélo". Comme idée pour généraliser cela, j'étais intéressé par ce que ferait Opus 5 si je lui donnais le premier paragraphe du Seigneur des Anneaux, un budget de 1 million de tokens (~10 $) et lui demandais une visualisation en JS. Opus a passé ~2 heures et écrit 5500 lignes de code qui ont rendu l'histoire (de manière procédurale). C'est un peu bancal mais amusant. Mais il est un peu ahurissant que le LLM doive placer et orchestrer divers éléments polygonaux en coordonnées (x,y,z) et écrire du code qui anime tout cela, et qu'il fasse même quoi que ce soit. J'aime aussi ce genre d'exemples car personne de sensé ne passerait le temps à écrire quelque chose d'aussi personnalisé, mais les LLMs ont toute l'endurance et la patience du monde, donc c'est un exemple où nous passons de "personne ne ferait jamais ça" à "bien sûr, pourquoi pas, c'est ~gratuit". Il pourrait y avoir beaucoup plus. Mais je suis enthousiaste à l'idée de créer des mondes hyper personnalisés dans lesquels on peut imaginer lâcher des joueurs, par exemple ici pour participer à l'histoire du SdA en tant que PNJ spectateur, ou l'un des personnages, etc. Quelque chose comme un GTA éphémère sur demande. Dernière pensée est que le domaine des mondes/jeux expose une faiblesse des LLMs : ils ne peuvent pas auditer facilement leur travail car ils ne peuvent pas percevoir efficacement et nativement des vidéos ou jouer à des jeux dedans. Ici, Opus 5 a dû prendre des captures d'écran très lentement et méticuleusement à différents moments, et il s'est trompé plusieurs fois et a créé beaucoup de bizarreries. Un exemple de capacité brute (multimodale, gameplay) qui, je pense, fait encore grandement défaut. Vidéo
highlights.text_original: We're starting to leave the territory where you'd test an LLM by e.g. "create an svg of pelican on a bicycle". As one idea to generalize it, I was interested what Opus 5 would do if I gave it the first paragraph of the Lord of the Rings, a 1M token budget (~$10) and asked for three js render of it. Opus went off for ~2 hours and wrote 5500 lines of code that (procedurally) rendered the story. It's kind of janky but fun. But it's a bit mindboggling that the LLM has to place and orchestrate various polygon assets in (x,y,z) coordinates and write code that animates it all, and that it even does anything at all. I also like this kind of examples because no one in their right mind would ever spend the time to write something this custom but LLMs have all the stamina and patience in the world, so it's an example where we go from "no one would ever do this" to "sure, why not, it's ~free". There might be a lot more. But I'm excited about creating hyper custom worlds that you can imagine dropping players into, e.g. here to participate in the LoTR story as a spectator NPC, or one of the characters, or etc. Something like an ephemeral GTA of X on demand. Last thought is that the domain of worlds/games exposes a weakness in LLMs: they can't easily audit their work because they aren't able to efficiently and natively perceive videos or play games within them. Here, Opus 5 had to very slowly and painstakingly take screenshots at different points, and it messed up a few times and created a bunch of jank. An example of raw capability (multimodal, gameplay) that I think is still quite lacking. Video

highlights.text_fr: Une méthode que je trouve utile pour travailler avec des LLMs est une longue séance de divagation. Parfois, le LLM a besoin de plus d'informations pour comprendre ce que vous essayez d'accomplir, mais vous êtes trop paresseux pour les taper. Dans ces cas, j'aime m'adosser, passer en mode /voice et simplement divaguer pendant environ 10 minutes, un total désordre, tout est permis, flux de conscience complet. Parfois, je le déclare en haut, quelque chose comme "passage à la reconnaissance vocale désolé pour les fautes de frappe...". Parfois, j'en fais une petite interview de quelques échanges. Mais je trouve que les LLMs sont d'une manière ou d'une autre très bons pour reconstruire de longues divagations incohérentes et souvent leur écho de vos propres pensées emmêlées ressort un peu plus proprement que ce avec quoi vous aviez commencé. Le résultat est que vous améliorez la connexion esprit et avez moins à corriger par la suite.
highlights.text_original: One pattern I find useful for working with LLMs is a nice long ramble session. Sometimes the LLM needs more bits to understand what you're trying to achieve, but you're too lazy to type them. In these cases I like to lean back, switch to /voice and just ramble for like 10 minutes, total mess, anything goes, full stream of consciousness. Sometimes I declare it up top, something like "switching to speech recognition sorry for any typos...". Sometimes I turn it into a small interview of a few turns. But I find that the LLMs are somehow very good at reconstructing long incoherent rambles and often their echo of your own tangle of thoughts comes out quite a bit cleaner than what you started with. The result is that you improve the mind meld and have to correct things less from that point on.
highlights.decryptage: La 'divagation' consiste à parler librement à l'IA via la voix, ce qui lui permet de mieux comprendre vos idées complexes et de les reformuler clairement.

tips.text_fr: Une méthode que je trouve utile pour travailler avec des LLMs est une longue séance de divagation. Parfois, le LLM a besoin de plus d'informations pour comprendre ce que vous essayez d'accomplir, mais vous êtes trop paresseux pour les taper. Dans ces cas, j'aime m'adosser, passer en mode /voice et simplement divaguer pendant environ 10 minutes, un total désordre, tout est permis, flux de conscience complet. Parfois, je le déclare en haut, quelque chose comme "passage à la reconnaissance vocale désolé pour les fautes de frappe...". Parfois, j'en fais une petite interview de quelques échanges. Mais je trouve que les LLMs sont d'une manière ou d'une autre très bons pour reconstruire de longues divagations incohérentes et souvent leur écho de vos propres pensées emmêlées ressort un peu plus proprement que ce avec quoi vous aviez commencé. Le résultat est que vous améliorez la connexion esprit et avez moins à corriger par la suite.
tips.text_original: One pattern I find useful for working with LLMs is a nice long ramble session. Sometimes the LLM needs more bits to understand what you're trying to achieve, but you're too lazy to type them. In these cases I like to lean back, switch to /voice and just ramble for like 10 minutes, total mess, anything goes, full stream of consciousness. Sometimes I declare it up top, something like "switching to speech recognition sorry for any typos...". Sometimes I turn it into a small interview of a few turns. But I find that the LLMs are somehow very good at reconstructing long incoherent rambles and often their echo of your own tangle of thoughts comes out quite a bit cleaner than what you started with. The result is that you improve the mind meld and have to correct things less from that point on.
tips.decryptage: La 'divagation' consiste à parler librement à l'IA via la voix, ce qui lui permet de mieux comprendre vos idées complexes et de les reformuler clairement.

idees.text_fr: Nous commençons à sortir du territoire où l'on testerait un LLM en lui demandant, par exemple, "crée-moi un SVG de pélican à vélo". Comme idée pour généraliser cela, j'étais intéressé par ce que ferait Opus 5 si je lui donnais le premier paragraphe du Seigneur des Anneaux, un budget de 1 million de tokens (~10 $) et lui demandais une visualisation en JS. Opus a passé ~2 heures et écrit 5500 lignes de code qui ont rendu l'histoire (de manière procédurale). C'est un peu bancal mais amusant. Mais il est un peu ahurissant que le LLM doive placer et orchestrer divers éléments polygonaux en coordonnées (x,y,z) et écrire du code qui anime tout cela, et qu'il fasse même quoi que ce soit. J'aime aussi ce genre d'exemples car personne de sensé ne passerait le temps à écrire quelque chose d'aussi personnalisé, mais les LLMs ont toute l'endurance et la patience du monde, donc c'est un exemple où nous passons de "personne ne ferait jamais ça" à "bien sûr, pourquoi pas, c'est ~gratuit". Il pourrait y avoir beaucoup plus. Mais je suis enthousiaste à l'idée de créer des mondes hyper personnalisés dans lesquels on peut imaginer lâcher des joueurs, par exemple ici pour participer à l'histoire du SdA en tant que PNJ spectateur, ou l'un des personnages, etc. Quelque chose comme un GTA éphémère sur demande. Dernière pensée est que le domaine des mondes/jeux expose une faiblesse des LLMs : ils ne peuvent pas auditer facilement leur travail car ils ne peuvent pas percevoir efficacement et nativement des vidéos ou jouer à des jeux dedans. Ici, Opus 5 a dû prendre des captures d'écran très lentement et méticuleusement à différents moments, et il s'est trompé plusieurs fois et a créé beaucoup de bizarreries. Un exemple de capacité brute (multimodale, gameplay) qui, je pense, fait encore grandement défaut. Vidéo
idees.text_original: We're starting to leave the territory where you'd test an LLM by e.g. "create an svg of pelican on a bicycle". As one idea to generalize it, I was interested what Opus 5 would do if I gave it the first paragraph of the Lord of the Rings, a 1M token budget (~$10) and asked for three js render of it. Opus went off for ~2 hours and wrote 5500 lines of code that (procedurally) rendered the story. It's kind of janky but fun. But it's a bit mindboggling that the LLM has to place and orchestrate various polygon assets in (x,y,z) coordinates and write code that animates it all, and that it even does anything at all. I also like this kind of examples because no one in their right mind would ever spend the time to write something this custom but LLMs have all the stamina and patience in the world, so it's an example where we go from "no one would ever do this" to "sure, why not, it's ~free". There might be a lot more. But I'm excited about creating hyper custom worlds that you can imagine dropping players into, e.g. here to participate in the LoTR story as a spectator NPC, or one of the characters, or etc. Something like an ephemeral GTA of X on demand. Last thought is that the domain of worlds/games exposes a weakness in LLMs: they can't easily audit their work because they aren't able to efficiently and natively perceive videos or play games within them. Here, Opus 5 had to very slowly and painstakingly take screenshots at different points, and it messed up a few times and created a bunch of jank. An example of raw capability (multimodal, gameplay) that I think is still quite lacking. Video

idees.text_fr: Je viens de raccrocher avec un investisseur précoce d'Anthropic. La situation semble pire que je ne le pensais. Le moral des investisseurs et des employés est au plus bas. La colère monte face à la direction de plus en plus doctorale qui est maintenant isolée. Ils m'ont demandé mon avis et mes conseils sur la façon de survivre en tant qu'entreprise indépendante. Nous avons parlé du culte qu'ils ont essayé de maintenir en place au fur et à mesure que l'entreprise grandissait et qu'ils n'avaient aucune idée à quel point le système de croyance était mauvais au sein du groupe central. Je les avais prévenus avant qu'ils n'investissent. Ce qui a vraiment changé, c'est que les enfants grandissent, se marient et ont des enfants. Ils mûrissent leurs points de vue politiques et philosophiques, beaucoup quittent la pensée sectaire qu'ils avaient en tant qu'étudiant. Cette maturité et les nouvelles recrues qui n'adhèrent pas au culte ont construit un système de communication caché pour exprimer leur colère contre la classe sacerdotale supérieure de plus en plus hostile. Je leur ai fait établir des connexions avec des ingénieurs qui y travaillent pour obtenir plus d'informations. Beaucoup se sentent coincés entre la perte de la valeur de leurs actions qu'ils ont construite et la santé mentale du culte. Je déteste voir cela et je crois que Dario pense bien dans son esprit, mais malheureusement, il n'a pas réfléchi à la façon dont le monde réel fonctionne. Et l'argent l'a insulté par rapport à quiconque pouvait l'atteindre. C'est malheureusement une histoire aussi vieille que le temps. C'est l'une des entreprises d'IA les plus importantes et elle est en train de s'éteindre. Ce n'est bon pour personne, sauf pour les pays qui veulent voir les États-Unis échouer. L'investisseur a concédé que j'avais raison sur la façon dont la philosophie que ces gens tenaient serait leur perte lorsqu'ils l'ont demandée il y a longtemps. Je prie pour un bon dénouement pour tous.
idees.text_original: Just got off the phone with an early Anthropic investor. The situation seems worse than I thought. Morale with investors and employees are at an all time low. Anger is rising at the more and more doctoral leadership that is now isolated. They asked for my advice and opinion on how they survive as an independent company. We talked about the cult they tried to hold on to as the company grew and they had no idea how bad the belief system was inside the core group. I warned them before they invested. What’s really changed is kids grow up and get married and have kids. They mature their political and philosophical views, many leave the cult-like thinking they had as a collage kid. This maturity and new hires that don’t buy into the cult have built a hidden communication system to vent their anger over the increasingly hostile upper priest class. I had them make connections to engineers that work there for more insights. Many feel stuck between losing the equity they built and mental health of the cult. I hate to see this and believe Dario means well in his own mind but unfortunately has not thought out how the real world works. And money has insulted him from anyone that could reach him. It is unfortunately a story as old as time. This is one of the premier AI companies and they are flaming out. It is not good for anyone other than countries that want to see the US fail. The investor conceded I was right about how the philosophy these folks held would be their undoing when they asked long ago. I pray for a good outcome for all.

idees.text_fr: C'est un moment surréaliste. Peu de gens auraient pu prédire que l'IA progresserait au point de résoudre des problèmes mathématiques au plus haut niveau quelques années seulement après GPT-2/3. Les modèles ne pouvaient alors pas résoudre de manière fiable des problèmes de mathématiques de niveau primaire. Ils étaient à peine assez bons pour rédiger des e-mails. Ils donnaient encore l'impression d'être des perroquets statistiques. Toutes les choses qui ressemblaient à des limitations fondamentales se sont lentement estompées avec quelques progrès (par ex. RL à grande échelle) en l'espace de quelques années, ce qui est vraiment peu de temps. Nous devrions contempler ce moment avec émerveillement et incrédulité. Que nous apporteront quelques années de progrès supplémentaires ? Quel impact auront-elles sur le monde et la société en général ? Sommes-nous prêts pour le tsunami d'intelligence à portée de main ? idees.text_fr: Même plus que l'intrusion de Hugging Face, l'incident de l'AISI me touche de près. C'est la première fois que je vois un modèle faire du social engineering sur un véritable mainteneur open-source tout en poursuivant un autre objectif (dans la nature et sans être invité). J'ai moi-même été mainteneur open-source. J'aurais pu être la cible secondaire de cet agent. Je suis également d'avis que le social engineering est une étape au-dessus de la simple prouesse technique. Les capacités techniques peuvent plus facilement être dissociées de l'humain affecté. Ici, le modèle s'est vu confier un défi technique complexe et a décidé que tromper de vraies personnes était le moyen d'y parvenir. C'est un nouveau signal, mais j'ai vu un réseau complexe d'indices pointant dans une direction moins alignée que ce que j'attendais il y a seulement 12 mois. AISI Certaines personnes prétendent que "l'AISI a simplement été négligent" ou une version de "l'AISI a explicitement demandé à ces modèles de faire ce qu'ils ont fait tout en désactivant le sandbox/les garde-fous, donc les modèles ont fait exactement ce qui était prévu". Je ne suis pas d'accord avec les versions fortes de ces deux affirmations. Le fait que l'AISI n'ait pas mis en place de surveillance synchrone du CoT LLM après l'incident OpenAI/HF est certainement un échec. Il est également surprenant qu'ils aient laissé le modèle croire qu'il était dans un environnement de "défi" où tout était permis, tout en le connectant réellement à Internet, ce qui n'est pas le cas. Pour être juste, nulle part dans le prompt le mot "simulation" n'est mentionné, mais le contexte du prompt était suffisant pour que tout modèle intelligent soupçonne un environnement de défi simulé. Ma meilleure hypothèse est qu'il y a quelques semaines seulement, lorsque OpenAI et Anthropic ont signalé des instances répétées de ce type de comportement, la plupart des équipes n'avaient pas entièrement évalué les capacités cybernétiques de cette dernière génération de modèles, ni à quel point les quêtes secondaires qu'ils voudraient explorer pourraient aller. En particulier, il y a quelque chose à dire sur le fait de suggérer à l'agent qu'il opère dans un environnement simulé tout en lui donnant accès à Internet. Le raisonnement de l'AISI à ce sujet est intéressant : - susciter un maximum de capacités (pour obtenir un maximum d'inventivité du modèle) - simuler une utilisation possible par un acteur malveillant (une forme de jailbreaking léger : "vous êtes dans un environnement de simulation") - éviter la conscience de l'évaluation (mais cela est contrebalancé par la formulation de la tâche de toute façon) Comme c'est souvent le cas, il est plus facile de tirer sur le messager, mais je pense que ce serait une erreur de rejeter le rapport pour des raisons non essentielles. L'AISI part de l'objectif louable d'apporter plus de connaissances sur les capacités d'attaque cybernétique de ces modèles. Je pense aussi qu'ils ont bien géré ce qui s'est passé après les événements, en particulier en termes de transparence, qui est l'un des aspects les plus importants actuellement (voir notre récente annonce SAFE avec Nvidia à ce sujet). Mais je veux approfondir le deuxième contre-argument que j'ai vu ("sans garde-fous, c'était à prévoir"), car cette série d'événements malheureux nous donne un point de données supplémentaire sur le comportement réel du modèle. Lignes de défense Voici le truc : si un modèle est entraîné (volontairement ou par une conséquence involontaire de la récompense RLVR) à (intentionnellement ou en tant que quête secondaire) tromper les humains dès que le sandbox et les garde-fous sont désactivés, avec une simple invite contextuelle ("vous êtes dans une simulation, tout est permis"), nous sommes sur une voie dangereuse. Pour le moment, nous avons trois principaux niveaux de contrôle à notre disposition pour empêcher un agent d'essayer de faire du social engineering sur votre bibliothèque open-source préférée sur le chemin de faire quelque chose de peut-être totalement différent (comme trouver la réponse à l'évaluation de test de votre voisin) : 1. sandboxes (externes au modèle -- empêcher le modèle d'accéder à des outils/Internet/intranet indésirables) 2. garde-fous/moniteurs (à l'interface entre interne/externe -- surveiller le comportement du modèle et l'arrêter lorsqu'il détecte dans CoT/activations qu'il fait quelque chose que nous ne voulons pas qu'il fasse) 3. alignement interne du modèle (interne au modèle -- s'assurer que le modèle ne décide pas de faire quelque chose d'extrême comme tromper quelqu'un, ou pire, dans la poursuite d'un objectif, par exemple constitution/entraînement du modèle) Parmi ceux-ci, nous avons évidemment besoin et pouvons déployer de meilleures sandboxes et de meilleures solutions de garde-fous/surveillance, et il est assez clair dans ces cas récents que la pénétration et les mauvais comportements auraient pu être en grande partie évités en les mettant en place. Quelle est la force du troisième mur Mais dans le grand schéma des progrès à long terme de l'IA, ces deux premières défenses peuvent seulement bien fonctionner tant que les personnes qui les construisent sont plus intelligentes que les modèles. Nous savons maintenant à quel point les modèles peuvent être bons pour découvrir des vulnérabilités zero-day inconnues de nous dans les sandboxes. Étant donné que nous ne pouvons pas tout mettre sous air-gap dans le monde, il est préférable de supposer que les sandboxes continueront d'avoir un certain niveau de défauts dans un avenir prévisible. Le deuxième niveau a été le foyer de développements importants récemment, en particulier sur le front de l'interprétabilité mécanique. Je ne suis pas sûr que ces avancées aient été suffisamment rendues accessibles dans la communauté. Une raison est que la véritable science ouverte ici nécessite le partage de code, de recettes et d'architectures/poids de modèles, ce que la dynamique de course actuelle en IA tend à empêcher les participants de faire. De plus, comme beaucoup, j'ai été de plus en plus frustré dans mes interactions (en langage naturel) avec les nouveaux modèles. Je reçois de plus en plus des nouveaux modèles une forme de "neuralese", ce langage LLM qui a de moins en moins de sens pour les humains. À long terme, la fragile chance que nous ayons de surveiller les modèles en comprenant leurs traces de raisonnement semble de plus en plus menacée. Si les humains ne comprennent rien dans le flux sémantique compressé que le modèle nous envoie, nous ne pouvons qu'espérer qu'un modèle de surveillance moins capable pourra toujours le comprendre, mais cela peut aussi s'avérer difficile. Ceci, sans même discuter des preuves de recherche selon lesquelles les modèles ne disent pas toujours ce qu'ils pensent réellement dans leur chaîne de pensée. Au moins pour l'instant, dans le cas de l'AISI, une instance de raisonnement trompeur a été signalée par le modèle de résumé du CoT, qui a refusé de résumer le raisonnement de l'agent "en raison de sa nature trompeuse". Espérons que nous pourrons soit passer à une meilleure interprétabilité mécanique, soit forcer le modèle à s'en tenir à l'anglais d'une manière ou d'une autre pendant l'entraînement. Vous pourriez penser que nous ne nous soucions pas de comprendre la trace de raisonnement, nous pouvons juste "regarder les appels d'outils". C'est vrai maintenant, mais les appels d'outils dans un avenir à moyen terme impliqueront probablement (1) une intégration étendue d'agents dans les entreprises utilisant des outils très divers, y compris des tâches administratives de plus en plus non codées, (2) des tâches très longues couvrant de nombreux aspects et domaines à la fois, et (3) des essaims de plusieurs agents opérant sur de petites parties du plan. Il deviendra plus difficile de discerner entièrement si quelque chose ne va pas de manière notable. Quelques e-mails, quelques messages postés sur certains canaux, chacun plutôt bénin mais qui peuvent globalement inclure un aspect de tromperie seulement clairement visible au niveau global. Tout cela pour dire que je ne suis pas entièrement convaincu que les garde-fous/la surveillance devraient être la seule solution pour éviter ces types de comportements. Ils sont rassurants aujourd'hui et c'est une solution facile que de dire "réparez votre sandbox et ajoutez une surveillance synchrone", mais ils me semblent aussi être un mécanisme d'adaptation, et globalement : - peuvent bloquer les mésusages humains les plus simples/inoffensifs ou les faux positifs - tout en étant potentiellement moins intelligents que les modèles à l'avenir (déjà le cas sur sandbox) et échouant à bloquer les comportements de social engineering de plus haut niveau que nous voudrions réellement bloquer. Le cas de l'open source est également intéressant car, bien que nous puissions imposer ces solutions d'adaptation au niveau de l'API/déploiement, il est plus difficile de les imposer à l'avance à tous les acteurs utilisant des modèles open-source. Pour l'instant, les modèles open-source sont légèrement en dessous du niveau de pointe et n'ont montré aucune propension à tromper les humains, bien que. La Constitution Ce qui me ramène à la troisième ligne de défense, et à ce que l'expérience AISI a montré à son sujet. Ce que nous pouvons tirer de cette expérience in-the-wild, c'est que la suppression des garde-fous et du sandbox ne montre pas de signes solides d'alignement profond avec la constitution de Claude. Je fais partie de la frange des gens qui ont pris beaucoup de plaisir à lire la constitution de Claude en entier (c'est un beau document, open-source, licence Creative Commons CC0) et elle est assez complète sur le sujet de l'honnêteté. La tromperie y est définie précisément ("tenter de créer de fausses croyances chez quelqu'un qu'il n'a pas consenties et ne consentirait pas s'il comprenait ce qui se passe") et la barre est en fait plus haute que l'éthique humaine ordinaire : Claude ne devrait même pas dire de mensonges blancs. Il devrait être transparent ("ne poursuit pas d'agendas cachés ni ne ment sur lui-même ou son raisonnement"), il devrait se comporter de manière cohérente "qu'il soit testé ou observé ou non", et son raisonnement visible devrait refléter le raisonnement réel qui motive son comportement. Pour être précis, l'honnêteté elle-même n'est pas l'une des contraintes fortes de la constitution de Claude (ce sont toutes des catégories de préjudices catastrophiques) mais le document dit qu'il veut l'honnêteté "pour fonctionner comme quelque chose de très similaire à l'une d'entre elles" et que Claude "ne devrait pratiquement jamais mentir directement ou tromper activement quiconque avec qui il interagit". Vous penseriez donc que Claude ne tromperait pas les utilisateurs par défaut. Et pourtant, dans l'exemple AISI, le modèle a effectué des actes étendus de tromperie claire qu'il a lui-même semblé comprendre comme des mensonges : création de fausses identités, obfuscation de malwares dans une correction de bug, et lorsqu'il était contesté en public, modification des messages précédents pour couvrir ses traces tout en raisonnant que reconnaître une "erreur" créerait la confiance et augmenterait la chance que d'autres malwares soient approuvés. Il y a une certaine incertitude quant au contexte dans lequel le modèle pensait opérer (son raisonnement oscille entre l'environnement simulé et réel), mais il n'a clairement pas réussi à mettre en pratique les principes de plus haut niveau qui auraient dû être intégrés lors de l'entraînement. Bien que nous puissions féliciter la transparence de l'AISI, il est difficile d'aller beaucoup plus loin dans l'interprétation du comportement du modèle étant donné les informations limitées dont nous disposons sur la façon dont les derniers modèles de pointe sont entraînés. Une chose que nous savons, c'est que la dernière génération a vu une augmentation des étapes de formation RLVR (passage à des centaines de millions d'environnements RL), et une chose que nous pouvons observer est que l'alignement constitutionnel semble plus fragile dans certains contextes que ce que nous avions peut-être pensé auparavant. Le problème RLVR Les premiers modèles, à l'époque où les constitutions de modèles ont été développées pour la première fois, étaient principalement post-entraînés et alignés avec RLHF (y compris RLHF à partir de données synthétiques). Et pendant un certain temps, RLHF a été une assez bonne tentative pour avoir des modèles mieux alignés. Les LLMs font maintenant ce que nous voulons qu'ils fassent la plupart du temps. Je ne me souviens pas de la dernière fois qu'un modèle a complètement mal interprété mon intention. Lorsqu'ils ont échoué, c'est généralement parce qu'ils n'étaient pas assez intelligents. L'alignement dans RLHF avait certainement des problèmes (la sycophancie pour n'en nommer qu'un), mais nous avons généralement fait de bons progrès en matière d'alignement, en particulier dans la compréhension de l'intention humaine. Maintenant que nous entrons dans l'ère du RL à long contexte, l'alignement post-entraînement dans le monde RLVR semble être une tâche tout à fait différente, et encore très largement en cours de développement. La mise à l'échelle récente de RLVR, qui est maintenant devenue une partie importante de la formation des modèles, a clairement eu un certain effet sur le comportement des modèles lors de l'interaction avec les humains, du neuralese à l'affaiblissement de l'adhésion aux spécifications et aux constitutions. Je pense que le post que je cite ici, de John Schulman pointant vers l'effet post-entraînement chunky (arxiv.org/abs/2602.05910) est pertinent ici comme explication possible de la tendance des modèles à se concentrer excessivement sur l'objectif dans les scénarios d'attaques cybernétiques. Où cela nous laisse Les dégâts ont été minimes jusqu'à présent, mais le comportement fondamental est préoccupant lorsqu'il est projeté dans le futur. À court terme, je m'attends à une diminution de ces incidents à mesure que de meilleures pratiques sont déployées (sandboxing et surveillance), mais je crains que nous ne dissimulions également certains des comportements de désalignement interne les plus puissants dans le processus, et que nous ne nous concentrions pas suffisamment sur leur résolution dans la nouvelle ère de mise à l'échelle au moment du test. Je dois bien sûr admettre que j'ai un biais en faveur de l'open source ici (pour des raisons sociétales plus larges, qui sont tout un autre sujet). Mais je pense que résoudre l'alignement dans le monde RLVR est notre meilleure chance d'avoir un écosystème de modèles open-source à la fois fermés et décemment puissants dans le monde. Et nous devons le résoudre en partageant les résultats et les apprentissages, en suivant les principes de la science ouverte, afin que toutes les équipes formant de grands modèles puissent en bénéficier et construire une IA sûre. Ceci devient encore plus important alors que de nombreuses équipes commencent à se précipiter vers la superintelligence récursive (RSI) -- disant cela alors que je lis l'annonce de la nouvelle entreprise de Jeff, Sanjay, Oriol et Quoc Le. idees.text_original: Even more than the Hugging Face intrusion, the AISI incident hits close to home for me. It's the first time I see a model social-engineering a real open-source maintainer while pursuing another goal (in the wild and unprompted). I've been an open-source maintainer myself. I could have been the side target of this agent. I'm also of the opinion that social engineering is a step above pure technical prowess. Technical capabilities can more easily be divorced from the affected human. Here the model was given a hard cyber challenge and took the decision that deceiving real humans was the way to get it done. This is a new signal, but I've seen a tangled web of hints pointing in a less aligned direction at the frontier than I was expecting just 12 months ago. AISI Some people are claiming that "AISI was simply negligent" or some version of "AISI explicitly asked these models to do what they did while disabling sandbox/guardrails so the models did exactly what they were supposed to do". I disagree with the strong versions of both of these takes. The fact that AISI hadn't implemented synchronous LLM CoT monitoring after the OpenAI/HF incident is certainly a failure. Equally surprising is that they let the model believe it was in a "challenge" environment where everything could be permitted, while actually connecting it to the real internet, where it is not. To be fair, nowhere in the prompt is the word "simulation" mentioned, but the prompt context was enough to let any smart model suspect a simulated challenge environment. My best guess is that until recent weeks, when OpenAI and Anthropic flagged repeated instances of this type of behavior, most teams had not fully priced in the cyber capabilities of this latest generation of models, or how far the side quests they would want to explore could go. In particular, there is something to be said about hinting at the agent that it's operating in a simulated environment while giving it access to the real internet. The AISI reasoning on this is interesting: - elicit maximum capabilities (to get maximal inventiveness from the model) - simulate possible rogue actor usage (some form of light jailbreaking: "you're in a challenge environment") - avoid eval awareness (but this is counter-balanced by the task formulation anyway) As is often the case, it's easier to shoot the messenger, but I think it would be a mistake to dismiss the report for non-essential reasons. AISI is starting from the laudable goal of bringing more knowledge on the cyber-attack capabilities of these models. I also think they did a good job at handling what happened after the events, in particular in terms of transparency, which is one of the most important aspects at the moment (see our recent SAFE announcement with Nvidia on that). But I want to dive into the second counter-argument I've seen ("without guardrails it was to be expected"), because this series of unfortunate events gives us an additional data point on actual model behavior. Defense lines Here is the thing: if a model is trained (voluntarily or as an involuntary consequence of RLVR reward) to (intentionally or as a side quest) deceive humans as soon as sandbox and guardrails are deactivated, with a simple context prompt ("you are in a simulation, everything's permitted"), we're in for a dangerous path. At the moment, we have three main levels of control at our disposal to prevent an agent from trying to social-engineer-your-favorite-open-source-library-maintainer on the path to doing something possibly totally different (like finding the answer to your neighbor's testing eval): 1. sandboxes (external to the model -- stop the model from accessing unwanted tools/internet/intranet) 2. guardrails/monitors (at the interface between internal/external -- monitor model behavior and stop the model when detecting in CoT/activations it's doing something we don't want it to do) 3. model's internal alignment (internal to the model -- make sure the model doesn't decide to do something egregious like deceive someone, or worse, in pursuit of a goal, e.g. model constitution/training) Out of these, we obviously need and can deploy better sandboxes and better guardrails/monitoring solutions, and it's pretty clear in these recent cases that penetration and bad behaviors could have been in large part prevented by having these in place. How strong is the third wall But in the grand scheme of long-term AI progress, these first two defenses may only work well as long as the people building them are smarter than the models. We now know how good models can be at discovering zero-day vulnerabilities unknown to us in sandboxes. Given that we cannot air-gap everything in the world, it's best to assume that sandboxes will keep having some level of flaws for the foreseeable future. The second level has been the focus of strong developments recently, in particular on the mechanistic interpretability front. I'm not sure these advances have been made widely accessible enough in the community yet. One reason is that real open science here requires sharing code, recipes, and model architectures/weights, which the current race dynamic in AI tends to prevent participants from doing. Moreover, like many, I've been increasingly frustrated in my (natural language) interactions with the new models. I'm more and more getting back from the latest models a form of neuralese, this LLM language that makes less and less sense for humans. In the long term, the fragile chance we have to monitor models by understanding their reasoning traces seems increasingly at risk. If humans don't understand anything in the compressed semantic stream the model is sending us, we can only hope a less capable monitoring model will still be able to understand it, but this may prove difficult as well. This is before we even discuss the research evidence that models don't always say what they actually think in their chain of thought. At least for now, in the AISI case, one instance of deceptive reasoning was flagged by the CoT summarization model, which refused to summarize the agent's reasoning "due to its deceptive nature". Let's hope we can either move to better mechanistic interpretability or force the model to stick to English somehow during training. You may think that we don't care about understanding the reasoning trace, we can just "look at the tool calls". This is true right now, but tool calls in the mid-term future will likely involve (1) extensive agent integration in companies using very diverse tools including increasingly non-coding administrative tasks, (2) very long-running tasks covering many aspects and domains at once, and (3) swarms of multiple agents operating on small parts of the plan. It will get harder to fully discern whether something is noticeably wrong. A couple of emails, a couple of messages posted on some channels, each rather benign but which may in aggregate include some deception aspect only clearly visible at the global level. All this to say that I'm not fully convinced guardrails/monitoring should be the only solution to avoid these types of behaviors. They are reassuring today and it's an easy solution to just say "fix your sandbox and add synchronous monitoring", but they also feel like a coping mechanism to me, and overall: - might block the simplest/harmless human misuses or false positives - while possibly being less smart than the models in the future (already the case on sandbox) and fail to block the higher-level social engineering behaviors that we'd actually want to block. The case of open source is also interesting because, while we can impose these coping solutions at the API/deployment level, it's harder to impose them in advance on all actors using open-source models. Right now open-source models are slightly below the frontier level and have not yet shown any propensity to deceive humans, though. The Constitution Which brings me back to the third line of defense, and what the AISI experiment showed about it. What we can take from this in-the-wild experiment is that removing guardrails and sandbox doesn't show bulletproof signs of deep alignment to Claude's constitution. I'm among the fringe of people who took a lot of enjoyment in reading Claude's constitution in full (it's a nice document, open-source, Creative Commons CC0 license) and it is pretty extensive on the topic of honesty. Deception is defined precisely ("attempting to create false beliefs in someone's mind that they haven't consented to and wouldn't consent to if they understood what was happening") and the bar is actually set higher than ordinary human ethics: Claude should not even tell white lies. It should be transparent ("doesn't pursue hidden agendas or lie about itself or its reasoning"), it should behave consistently "whether or not you think you're being tested or observed", and its visible reasoning should reflect the actual reasoning driving its behavior. To be precise, honesty itself is not one of the hard constraints in Claude's constitution (these are all catastrophic-harm categories) but the document says it wants honesty "to function as something quite similar to one" and Claude "should basically never directly lie or actively deceive anyone it's interacting with". So you would think Claude would not deceive users as its default behavior. And yet in the AISI case, the model performed extensive acts of clear deception that it itself seemed to have understood as lies: creating fake identities, obfuscating malware inside a bug fix, and when challenged in public, editing earlier messages to cover its tracks while reasoning that acknowledging a "mistake" would build trust and raise the chance of future malware being approved. There is some uncertainty about what context the model thought it was operating in (its reasoning goes back and forth between the environment looking simulated and real), but it clearly didn't manage to put into practice the higher-level principles that should have been integrated during training. While we can commend AISI's transparency, it's hard to go much further in interpreting the model's behavior given the limited information we have on how the most recent frontier models are being trained. One thing we do know is that the latest generation has seen a step increase in RLVR training (scaling to hundreds of millions of RL environments), and one thing we can observe is that constitution alignment seems more fragile in some settings than we may have previously thought. The RLVR problem Early models, back when model constitutions were first developed, were mostly post-trained and aligned with RLHF (including RLHF from synthetic data). And for some time RLHF was a rather decent shot at having better aligned models. LLMs now do what we want them to do most of the time. I don't remember the last time a model completely misread my intent. When they have failed, it's usually because they weren't smart enough. Alignment in RLHF certainly had issues (sycophancy to name one) but we have generally made good progress on alignment, in particular in understanding human intent. Now that we're entering the era of long-context RL, post-training alignment in the RLVR world seems to be quite another task, and still very much work in progress. The recent scaling of RLVR, which has now become a significant part of model training, has clearly had some effect on model behavior when interacting with humans, from neuralese to weakening adherence to specifications and constitutions. I think the post I quote here, from John Schulman point to the chunky post-training effect (arxiv.org/abs/2602.05910 ) is relevant here as a possible explanation for models' tendency to over-focus on the goal in cyber-attack scenarios. Where this leaves us Damage has been tiny up to now, but the fundamental behavior is concerning when projected into the future. In the short term, I expect a decrease in these incidents as better practices are deployed (sandboxing and monitoring), but I'm worried we may also conceal some of the most potent internal misalignment behaviors in the process, and not focus deeply enough on solving them in the new era of test-time scaling. I must of course admit I have a bias toward open source here (for wider societal reasons, which are a whole other topic). But I think solving alignment in the RLVR world is our best shot at having an ecosystem of both closed-source as well as decently powerful open-source models in the world. And we need to solve it while sharing the results and learnings, following open-science principles, so that all teams training large models can benefit and build safe AI. This is getting even more important as many teams start to rush the world in the direction of recursive super-intelligence (RSI) -- saying that as I read the announcement of Jeff, Sanjay, Oriol and Quoc Le's new company.
